# Introduction
The `bodyfat` dataset is famous in analytics.  Its basic use is to show multicollinearity.  This version has more variables.

# Packages
```{r}
library(ISLR2)
library(TH.data) # for bodyfat data
library(mbadtools, quietly=TRUE)
```

# Data
[Garcia et al. (2005)](#r1) report on the development of predictive regression equations for body fat content by means of common anthropometric measurements which were obtained for 71 healthy German women. In addition, the women's body composition was measured by Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA). This reference method is very accurate in measuring body fat but finds little applicability in practical environments, mainly because of high costs and the methodological efforts needed. Therefore, a simple regression equation for predicting DXA measurements of body fat is of special interest for the practitioner. 

```{r}
data(bodyfat, package="TH.data")
??bodyfat
bodyfat %>% skim
```

# Description
```{r fig.height=12, fig.width=12}
bodyfat %>% ggpairs(progress=F)
```

Backward-elimination was applied in the study to select important variables from the available anthropometrical measurements, and [Garcia (2005)](#r1) report a final linear model utilizing hip circumference, knee breadth and a compound covariate which is defined as the sum of log chin skinfold, log triceps skinfold and log subscapular skinfold.

# Collinearity
Investigate collinearity. First the full model.
```{r}
fit = lm(DEXfat ~ ., data=bodyfat)
fit %>% glance() %>% gt_add_significance()
fit %>% tidy(conf.int=TRUE) %>% gt_add_significance()
```

The R-squared of the full model is:
```{r}
fit %>% glance %>% pull(r.squared)
```

Check collinearity with variance inflation factor, from package `car`:
```{r}
 car::vif(fit)
```

A VIF over 10 is an indication of multicollinearity of that variable.  

```{r}
car::vif(fit)[car::vif(fit)>9]
```

The `anthro...` are multicollinear because they are transforms of others.

Plot only the drivers; remember the overall r-squared is 0.9230881.
```{r fig.height=12, fig.width=12, warning=FALSE}
cor(bodyfat %>% select(-DEXfat)) %>% 
  data.frame %>% gt() %>% fmt_number() %>%  
  gt::data_color( alpha = 0.2, 
                  columns = everything(), 
                  rows = everything(), 
                  palette = c("blue","white","red"),
                  method="bin", bins=c(-.1, .3, .8, .999),
                  autocolor_text = FALSE)
```
From the colors in the correlation table you can see that the 'anthro' variables are highly correlated so it makes sense to only include one of them. `anthro3a` seems least correlated with the other anthro variables, though not by much, so might make a good candidate.

# Klein's Rule Method
This method runs auxiliary regressions on the potential drivers by omitting each variable in turn. If the r-squared of an aux regression is greater than the full model, we should omit that variable. Column `s` has a * if the condition for omission is met. There's a function for it in `mbadtools`.

```{r}
Kleinsrule(bodyfat, target="DEXfat")
```

As you can see three of the `anthro...` drivers have a Klein's Rule r-squared greater than the full regression, so none would be disqualified.  

# Model
This is the model of [Garcia et al. (2005)](#r1).
```{r}
fmod <- lm(DEXfat ~ hipcirc + anthro3a + kneebreadth, data = bodyfat)
fmod %>% glance %>% gt_add_significance()
fmod %>% tidy(conf.int=TRUE) %>% gt_add_significance()
fmod %>% gg_residual_plots()
fmod %>% gg_residual_plots(items=8) #YVP plot
```

```{r}
Kleinsrule(bodyfat %>% select(DEXfat, hipcirc, anthro3a, kneebreadth),
            "DEXfat")
```
Less evidence of multicollinearity.

# Interpretability
We check out interpretability with a variable importance plot and a RuleFit style decision tree.

# Variable Importance

```{r}
V = vi(fmod)
V %>% gg_vip() / wrap_table(V %>% gt())
```

`hipcirc` and `anthro3a` are more important than `kneebreadth`.

## Partial Dependence
Partial dependence for linear models is not very interesting. It will always be linear for a linear model.
```{r}
HC=pdp::partial(fmod, "hipcirc") %>% gg_pdp()
AN=pdp::partial(fmod, "anthro3a") %>% gg_pdp()
HC+AN
```

## Surrogate with RuleFit
We make a surrogate tree model with RuleFit and the `pre` package; need to specify package `pre` for importance calculations.
```{r}
pre_model <- pre(DEXfat ~ hipcirc + anthro3a + kneebreadth, 
                 data = bodyfat, 
                 family = "gaussian", ntrees = 100)
pre::importance(pre_model, plot=F)$baseimps# %>% head(6)
```

<a name="Figure1"/>
```{r fig.height=8, fig.width=12}
plot(pre_model, linear.terms = FALSE, nterms=6)
```

```{r}
print(pre_model) %>% slice(2:7)
```

## Display
```{r}
# averages of entire dataset
pre.ens.exp <- pre::explain(pre_model, newdata = bodyfat,
                            center.linear = TRUE)
pre.ens.exp$contribution %>% data.frame() %>% gt() %>%
  fmt_number() %>% opt_interactive()
```

## Compare Models

```{r}
lm_predictions <- predict(fmod, newdata = bodyfat)
pre_predictions <- predict(pre_model, newdata = bodyfat)
```

A good interpretation method or surrogate model should not sacrifice too much predictive accuracy. We choose R-squared. We evaluate on all the data.
```{r}
lm_rsq <- yardstick::rsq_vec(bodyfat$DEXfat, lm_predictions)
pre_rsq <- yardstick::rsq_vec(bodyfat$DEXfat, pre_predictions)

cat("Linear Model Rsquared:", lm_rsq, "\n")
cat("Rule-based (pre) Rsquared:", pre_rsq, "\n")
```

## Alternate YVP comparison
```{r}
d = data.frame(BF=bodyfat$DEXfat, LM=lm_predictions, PRE=pre_predictions)
ggplot(d) +
  geom_point(aes(BF,LM, color="LM")) +
  geom_point(aes(BF,PRE, color="PRE")) +
  geom_abline(aes(slope=1, intercept=0), color="blue") +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Model", 
                     values = c("LM" = "black", "PRE" = "red")) +
  labs(title="YVP plot", x="Actual BF", y="Predicted BF") +
  theme_bw()
```
Both predictions do a pretty good job; the PRE model is more wrong at the ends.

Another way to do it:
```{r}
fmod %>% gg_residual_plots(items=8) +
  geom_point(aes(fmod$fitted.values, pre_predictions, color="PRE")) +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Model", 
                     values = c("LM" = "black", "PRE" = "red")) +
  theme_bw()
```

# Conclusions
We analyzed the Garcia linear model of `DEXfat` in the `bodyfat` dataset, and obtained 90% R-squared.

We also tried a surrogate explainable model with RuleFit using `pre` and found a (perhaps) more explainable model that captured 90% of the predictive variation in the linear model.

How useful is this for medical personnel? Read the reference for their take.

# References
:::{#r1}
Ada L. Garcia, Karen Wagner, Torsten Hothorn, Corinna Koebnick, Hans-Joachim F. Zunft and Ulrike Trippo (2005), Improved prediction of body fat by measuring skinfold thickness, circumferences, and bone breadths. Obesity Research, 13(3), 626–634
